title: Burst resilience harness playground
content:
Purpose:
This is a working notebook for exploring microburst / short-burst resilience in the throughput harness. Goal is to capture pragmatic loadgen configurations, heuristics for repeatability, and a set of small, cheap experiments that expose hidden bottlenecks (scheduler stalls, KV cache contention, batching starvation) that larger steady-state benchmarks miss.

Context / motivation:
- We have lots of steady-state ramp/plateau runs; those mask transient failure modes customers hit (sudden spike from UI, chat multiprompting, system retries).
- Need cheap, repeatable experiments that exercise the runtime's ability to absorb bursts without violating tail SLAs.
- This doc belongs in the serving-runtime playbook family but intentionally informal — playground for rapid iteration.

Definitions we use here (short):
- microburst: arrivals concentrated in 50ms-5s window with aggregate QPS > 2x baseline for that window.
- effective batching: how many tokens or requests are coalesced on the device per scheduling quantum.
- occupancy: fraction of GPU compute queue filled by active sequences measured over 1s windows.
- priming/warmup: sequence of traffic intended to populate KV caches, JIT kernels, and GPU microstates.

Quick checklist for an experiment run (1–2 person 30–90m):
- Pick host and model (g4dn-16-like, gpus: A10/4090/RTX6000) + model size (7b/13b/3b).
- Clear runtime caches / restart worker to reproduce cold-start baseline.
- Define baseline sustained QPS from steady-state bench.
- Create burst profile: amplitude (x2/x5/x20), duration (100ms/1s/10s), spacing (single/periodic).
- Select client pattern: closed-loop (wait for response), open-loop (fire-and-forget), or mixed.
- Run 3 repeats with the same seed/inputs and collect logs + perf counters.

Example loadgen snippets (text form, adapt into loadgen config):
- short single-shot microburst (open-loop):
  concurrency: 200
  arrival_pattern: fixed-interval 0.01s (100 qps client)
  burst_window: 0.15s -> scale to achieve 2k requests in 150ms
  payload: single short prompt (15 tokens)
  repeat: 3 runs, 30s quiet between runs

- periodic microburst train (mixed):
  train_count: 10
  burst_interval: 5s
  burst_profile: 500req @ 200ms
  background_qps: 25
  client_mode: open-loop with 20 worker threads per client machine

Warmup recipe we converged on (cheap and pragmatic):
- Stage 0: cold worker restart. Wait 10s for health checks.
- Stage 1: lightweight priming (2x baseline qps for 30s) using short prompts to populate kernels.
- Stage 2: KV warm (client-driven multi-prompt per session) run 60s to seed KV caches with typical tokens/frames.
- Stage 3: amplitude probe: 3 bursts at 1.5x baseline to confirm no scheduling anomalies.
- Wait 20s, record baseline metrics.
Notes: skipping stage 2 often changes tail behavior for chat workloads under bursty traffic.

Observability signals to capture (essentials):
- infra: node CPU%, GPU util %, GPU memory, nvlink traffic (if available), thermal sensors.
- runtime: request enqueue delay, scheduling quantum latency, batch size distribution, worker queue length, active sessions, KV cache hit ratio.
- app-layer: per-request token count, time-to-first-byte (TTFB), completion latency, p50/p90/p99/p999.
- traces: remote spans for client->router->worker. 

Why repeats + seeds matter here (short note to self):
- Burst experiments are high-variance: small differences in client scheduling or network delay shift queuing across worker boundaries and change batching composition. Using seeds and repeat schedule makes it possible to correlate anomalies to system events (GC, thermal throttling).

Small experiment log (iteration notes):
- 2025-02-18: test A (A10 13b), single-shot 5000req/200ms window. Result: p99 increased by 4x vs baseline; GPU util spiked but batch sizes shrank during window. Hypothesis: scheduler hit max batch size quickly then serializes smaller requests -> batching starvation.
- 2025-02-20: test B, enabled client-side request coalescing (grouping 3 prompts per request). Result: tail latency partially recovered; effective tokens/sec better by 18%. Note: affects semantics, not always acceptable.
- 2025-02-23: test C, added 1s background sustained qps(25) + periodic 500req bursts. Observed long-tailed queueing at worker ingress; queue length asymmetry across workers. Traced to sticky session routing creating imbalanced hotspots.
- 2025-02-27: test D, tuned router fanout to prefer round-robin for burst windows -> reduced worker hot spots and p99 improved ~22%.

Anomalies / gotchas we've seen:
- Thermal cliffing: GPUs with higher baseline temps show poorer burst absorption (observed on two racks). Short-run thermal throttling can start within 20–60s under repeated bursts.
- Kernel JIT cold path: when a particular sequence length combination hasn't been seen recenty, the first few requests take much longer. Warmup must include diverse lengths.
- KV collision storms: many simultaneous sessions trying to update the same cached key subset cause short lock contention in the KV layer; appears as serialized requests at the worker kernel.
- Client clock skew: small skews across client machines create micro-staggering that either smoothes or amplifies bursts depending on offset. Reproducibility suffers without NTP/clock sync.

Hypotheses to validate (next experiments):
- H1: adaptively increasing batch window during high ingress reduces p99 at cost of slight p50 degradation. Experiment: dynamic batch window + burst detector.
- H2: router-level short-term randomized routing (jittered round-robin) reduces hotspot variance vs pure hashing on session id.
- H3: introducing lightweight request coalescing at gateway (combine <N small prompts queued within 50ms) improves throughput for chat UIs while keeping semantic correctness for many workloads.

Quick experiment scripts (examples):
- replay.sh (pseudo):
  ./loadgen --config burst.json --seed 2342 --out /tmp/run-2342 --dump-metrics
  tail -f /tmp/run-2342/metrics.log | tee /tmp/run-2342/annotated.log
- metrics-collect (pseudo):
  for node in $NODES; do ssh $node 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv' >> /tmp/run-2342/gpu.csv; done

Logging hygiene and artifacts to store per run:
- loadgen config JSON (full) + client machine list + seed
- router logs (time-synced) + worker perf counters
- aggregated metrics (prometheus scrape) and raw perf events
- sample request ids for requests falling into p99/p999 buckets (for trace lookup)

Repro strategy summary (rules of thumb):
- Always include a small quiet window before a burst to ensure baseline stabilization.
- Use the same number of client machines and thread counts across repeats. Document them in run metadata.
- Keep client clocks in sync; prefer containerized loadgen with fixed CPU affinity.
- Capture system-level counters to disambiguate thermal vs scheduling issues.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add automatic detection of worker hot-spotting in the harness and emit recommendations for router policy changes. (todo: prototype detector)
- Document a standard mini-burst profile for cross-team comparisons. (todo: propose one: 500req@200ms, 1s spacing, 5 repeats)
- Integrate a cheap KV-contention synthetic that can be toggled in harness to surface lock storms.
- Run same microburst profiles on quantized vs fp16 paths to compare scheduling characteristics.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep experiments small and fast — long 30m runs are great for release validation but kill iteration speed.
- When p99 shifts wildly between repeats, look for infra events (kube evictions, node autoscaling, thermal alarms). Also check router logs for sudden rebalances.
- Share promising mitigations with solutions-eng; customers frequently prefer gateway-side fixes (coalescing, retries) to model changes.

Appendix: quick param glossary
- open-loop: loadgen doesn't wait for responses before sending next request (stressful).
- closed-loop: client waits for each response (backpressures the system).
- fanout: number of workers the router attempts for a request; high fanout increases chance to find idle worker but increases network overhead.

End of playground note. Keep iterating.
